The Middle East conflict has roiled global shipping, sending governments and shipping firms scrambling to seek alternative routes. Sailing from Busan New Port, container ship PanStar Acro would sail to Europe via the Arctic, testing whether a route opened by melting sea ice could be commercially viable. The container ship Panstar Acro is anchored at Busan New Port in South Korea yesterday. Photo: AFP “The ship will depart at 8pm today unless there are unforeseen circumstances, such as bad weather,” a South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries official said. The ship would leave for Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland before returning, with the voyage expected to take about 45 days, the ministry said. The voyage follows that of the Chinese container ship Dubai Tower, which left the eastern port city of Ningbo for Europe this month, heading north through the Bering Strait before turning west along Russia’s Arctic coast. The usual maritime route between Asia and Europe runs through the Suez Canal, but traveling through the Arctic could cut the journey by about 7,000km and about 10 days, the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy said. South Korean Vice Minister of Oceans and Fisheries Nam Jae-hon said the Arctic route was “bound to become an alternative” to Middle Eastern shipping lanes — as geopolitical risks and technological advances make it increasingly competitive. Arctic University of Norway political science professor Marc Lanteigne said the voyage — coming soon after Dubai Tower began its own Arctic journey — showed that the Northern Sea Route was becoming normalized as a “secondary maritime transit corridor.” A successful voyage would demonstrate South Korea’s interest in “developing alternative shipping sea lanes,” he said, adding that it could fall behind as Chinese firms expand regular services through the increasingly viable Arctic route. Some experts warned that South Korean ships using the Arctic route could risk breaching Western sanctions on Russia, as they would receive Russian navigation and weather services involving payments, albeit small ones. The South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs declined to comment about the concerns involving Russia. The oceans ministry said this week that “consultations with key relevant countries and agencies” have been completed to “implement administrative procedures necessary” for the voyage. University of Oslo Korean studies professor Vladimir Tikhonov said: “strictly speaking, US and EU sanctions are not international law, unlike UN sanctions.” “And with continued uncertainty in the Middle East — itself driven in part by US actions — South Korea may have few alternatives if the Arctic route proves economically viable,” he said. Lanteigne said China’s Northern Sea Route ambitions were more politically driven than South Korea’s, with Beijing viewing the polar regions as “strategic new frontiers,” raising Western security concerns. Meanwhile, environmental groups warned growing traffic along the shorter route could accelerate Arctic sea ice loss already driven by global warming. Major carriers including CMA CGM, MSC and Hapag-Lloyd have pledged to avoid Arctic shipping routes. What we know on day 1,722 Guardian staff and agencies Tue 10 Nov 2026 20.08 EST Last modified on Tue 10 Nov 2026 20.27 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has backed Ukraine’s assessment of what is happening on the battlefield and that Vladimir Putin lives in a “different reality” , as American-led trilateral discussions between Ukraine, ⁠Russia and the US got under way in Abu Dhabi. In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said that Russia has claimed at the talks that they occupied half of the Donbas in Ukraine’s east. “This is the problem. Putin lives in a different reality,” the Ukrainian president wrote, adding “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield.” Zelenskyy said he was “happy” to see a change in the approach by US mediators at the Abu Dhabi talks. “I see changes. I’m very happy with what I hear. We will see what can be done,” Zelenskyy told a press conference in Copenhagen after being asked about changes in the approach to peace talks made by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Zelenskyy described the first day of talks – the first three-sided discussions to be held since February – as constructive and substantive . He said the agenda in Abu Dhabi had included formulating a new security architecture for Europe, an idea raised earlier on Tuesday by Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100% what they want. I think we understand, but nobody ​saw the documents, what the Americans discussed with the Russians,” Zelenskyy said. In Abu Dhabi, US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war, Andrew Roth and Jennifer Rankin report . Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said, but European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence. Ukraine’s foreign minister said he ⁠had urged US secretary of state Marco Rubio to accelerate ⁠interceptor ​deliveries as Russia ramps up attacks on energy ⁠infrastructure. Speaking to Reuters after talks ​with Rubio, Andrii Sybiha said he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took ‌place in Abu Dhabi. He said Ukraine remained prepared to ​discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure. Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine , triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month, Jennifer Rankin reports from Brussels. The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort. “What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister , Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava, alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. Latvia ⁠and Lithuania warned people across several regions to take shelter due ⁠to threats ⁠of ​unidentified drones entering their airspace via neighbouring Russia or Belarus early on Wednesday. Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre said its warning included ⁠the country’s second city of Kaunas, which has ​a population of about ‌300,000 people. As ‌Ukraine attacks Russia’s Baltic Sea oil shipping ports, some of its drones have ​missed their targets and led to security warnings in neighbouring countries. Moscow ⁠has accused Kyiv of using Nato airspace ​as cover ​for attacks, while Kyiv ​says some of its drones have ​been steered off ‌course by Russian ​signal ​jamming. The Nato countries blame Russia for the incidents, saying it ignited the war.
